Cellular respiration breaks down glucose in three stages, with NADH and FADH2 carrying electrons to the ATP-producing final stage.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm without oxygen and splits one six-carbon glucose into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules.
Glycolysis consumes 2 ATP and 2 NAD+ and produces 4 ATP and 2 NADH, for a net yield of 2 ATP per glucose.
Pyruvate oxidation, also called the link reaction, converts pyruvate into two-carbon acetyl-CoA in mitochondria and produces 2 CO2 and 2 NADH but no ATP per glucose.

The Krebs cycle is also called the citric acid cycle and occurs in the mitochondrial matrix; acetyl-CoA combines with four-carbon oxaloacetate to form six-carbon citrate before oxaloacetate is regenerated.
The Krebs cycle turns twice per glucose, consumes 2 acetyl-CoA, 6 NAD+ and 2 FAD, and produces 4 CO2, 6 NADH, 2 FADH2 and 2 ATP.
The electron transport chain occurs in the inner mitochondrial membrane, whose folds are called cristae.
Electron transfer pumps hydrogen ions from the matrix into the intermembrane space; their return through ATP synthase produces ATP by chemiosmosis.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and forms water; without oxygen, electron transport stops and the Krebs cycle subsequently stops because NAD+ is depleted.
The electron transport stage consumes 10 NADH, 2 FADH2, oxygen, ADP and phosphate and yields recycled NAD+ and FAD, water and about 26–28 ATP.
Glycolysis and Krebs-cycle ATP are made by substrate-level phosphorylation, whereas electron-transport ATP is made by oxidative phosphorylation.
The total yield is about 30–32 ATP per glucose; older textbook totals of 36–38 use higher estimates of ATP produced per NADH and FADH2.
